transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-08-14
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Maria Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramírez (SE), Alex Park (Aegis ML), Samira Khan (CTO), Jordan Lee (SRE)

Summary (auto): They see repeated KV cache evictions when running 512k+ token sessions; suspect prefix reuse plus batch reshuffling and quantization alignment is causing fragmentation and unexpected paging.

[00:00] Maria: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros?
[00:10] Alex: Yeah Alex Park, works on our inference infra. we run models for long multi-turn logs, uh 200k to 1M token sessions per user in some cases.
[00:20] Samira: Samira, CTO. we're trying to stabilize latency regen under heavy long context.
[00:28] Maria: Great, and Diego from our performance team will run through the runtime details.
[00:36] Diego: Hi all, thanks. quick agenda: we'll cover how the KV cache is laid out in memory, eviction heuristics, paging to host, effects of quantization rounding on kv size, and then look at the traces you sent.
[00:50] Jordan: we uploaded a couple of logs to the S3 link, there's a few OOMs and some spike in tail latency around 60-120 seconds into sessions.
[01:05] Diego: cool, let's jump in. first: our KV cache keeps per-layer key/value tensors per sequence position. we allocate a contiguous buffer per model shard and keep an LRU-ish pointer for eviction. (note: transcript may show small omissions)
[01:25] Alex: we've seen kv "evictons" — spelled wrong in some logs — basically tokens disappearing and then regen expensive recomputation.
[01:35] Diego: right. eviction happens when the buffer hits high watermark then we evict oldest prefixes. but two things can complicate this: prefix reuse and batching.
[01:46] Samira: what do you mean by prefix reuse? can you give an example?
[01:50] Diego: sure. prefix reuse is when many requests share the same initial context (like system prompts or conversation history) and we dedupe at a routing layer, however if two requests come in with slightly different offsets we end up storing duplicate kv segments. that duplicates memory footprint and increases eviction pressure.
[02:08] Alex: oh that explains some patterns, we do large reused prompts but occasionally inject per-customer metadata at token 10 which leads to slight divergence.
[02:18] Maria: common pattern; we've seen customers unintentionally defeat prefix caching with tiny per-session tokens.
[02:24] Jordan: also note we use 4-bit quantization for bigger models to save memory. could that affect cache sizing?
[02:31] Diego: yes, quantization changes per-parameter bytes and alignment; 4-bit packs can still leave padding per warp/chunk and when we page kv out to host it rounds up. with hybrid quant and mixed precision, effective KV size isn't always straightforward.
[02:49] Alex: in our logs, eviction mostly happens during bursts when many batched requests reach different endpoints. is batching causing reshuffle?
[02:57] Diego: batching amplifies the issue. if the batcher groups slightly different contexts together, we materialize all their distinct kv sequences in memory simultaneously. additionally our continuous batching algorithm can reorder requests which prevents ideal prefix reuse.
[03:13] Samira: is there a tuning knob on batcher or on eviction thresholds we can tweak?
[03:19] Diego: yes. two immediate knobs: batch_max_tokens and batch_time_ms to reduce cross-context aggregation; and cache_high_watermark and eviction_granularity for the runtime to evict in larger aligned blocks to reduce fragmentation. Maria: we'll share recommended ranges.
[03:36] Jordan: about paging: when KV doesn't fit we page to host and then stream back; we're seeing elevated tail latencies during those periods. any ways to predict when paging will happen?
[03:46] Diego: we expose metrics: kv_allocated_bytes, kv_active_positions, kv_pages_in_use, and page_fault_count. if kv_allocated / total_buffer > .85 you get into risk zone. set alerting on page_fault_count.
[03:58] Alex: our alert shows page_fault spikes correlate with user sessions > ~300k tokens.
[04:05] Diego: that fits. the runtime assumes typical sequence distribution; extremely long contiguous sessions push beyond design point and we start triaging by evicting prefixes which can then cause re-compute if requests need that context later.
[04:20] Samira: can we configure per-tenant pinning? some customers are single-tenant and need their sessions pinned in cache longer.
[04:27] Maria: yes Dedicated and Private deployments support per-tenant reservation and pin-size. we can also pin certain prefix hashes to avoid eviction.
[04:36] Jordan: if we pin too much, we could starve others. is there a fair-share policy?
[04:41] Diego: we have a token-weighted allocator; you can set tenant quanta. default is proportional to recent usage, but you can override with hard caps.
[04:51] Alex: quick question on prefix hashing collisions — could those cause wrong reuse?
[04:56] Diego: we use 128-bit content hashes; collisions are effectively negligible. more common is near-duplicates where small token diffs produce different hashes.
[05:07] Samira: any known issues with quantized kernels that blow up memory transiently?
[05:12] Diego: occasionally. when kernels align to GPU memory pages or tensor cores, padded allocations increase temporary footprint during matmuls. especially on older drivers. updating drivers and using our tuned kernels helps.
[05:26] Alex: we run on-prem in VPC with custom NICs; are there network implications when paging to host?
[05:32] Diego: yes, paging streams over PCIe to host memory or NVLink; if you're in a VPC/on-prem with model pinned on local devices, network shouldn't be in the loop. but with remote host paging (e.g., host memory on different node) it can cross the interconnect and add latency.
[05:49] Jordan: logs show occasional 200–400ms spikes during page-in.
[05:54] Diego: that sounds like page-in over NVMe or remote host; look for device_attach/release in the trace.
[06:01] Maria: we've prepared a sample perf capture and dockerized profiler to collect KV metrics, will share.
[06:07] Alex: great. what about prefix reuse patterns—any heuristic to de-duplicate near-duplicates?
[06:12] Diego: we have a configurable prefix-trie approach: you can set minimal match length or token fuzzy thresholds. for near-duplicates you can enable approximate dedupe which will canonicalize similar prefixes into single KV segments with a small mismatch penalty on attention masks. it's experimental but helps in high-reuse corpuses.
[06:33] Samira: is that safe for privacy? deduping across tenants could leak context.
[06:39] Diego: absolutely — only safe within tenant scope and with opt-in. for shared hosted we don't enable cross-tenant dedupe. in private/dedicated you can enable it and optionally encrypt dedupe keys.
[06:52] Jordan: our cluster sees fluid batch sizes; sometimes we observe eviction of the middle of a sequence, not just oldest prefixes. is that possible?
[06:59] Diego: eviction of middle is symptomatic of fragmentation. if your allocator cannot find a contiguous block for a new kv append, it may evict older blocks out of order or do block compaction which looks like middle eviction.
[07:12] Alex: we have a dump that shows fragmentation increasing over time. is there a compaction routine?
[07:18] Diego: yes but it's expensive; we run background compaction during low-util windows. you can also increase eviction_granularity to force evictions in aligned chunks which reduces fragmentation.
[07:31] Samira: can you walk through a concrete timeline example where prefix reuse + batch reorder causes evictions?
[07:35] Diego: yes, imagine 3 requests A,B,C share prompt P; A diverges at token 8, B at token 9, C at token 12. If batcher groups B and C with different offsets, both diverging seqs are materialized; if memory tight, oldest P might be kept but the small divergent tails are evicted first leading to re-compute when similar later requests come back. Also if batcher reorders a request with older context behind a large new request, the allocator must make room and may evict live prefixes.
[08:04] Jordan: what's our recommended config for heavy long-context workloads?
[08:08] Diego: baseline: set cache_high_watermark to 0.9, cache_low_watermark to 0.6, eviction_granularity to 64KB chunks, enable approx-dedupe for tenant-local reuse, and reduce batch_time_ms to 20ms with batch_max_tokens lowered. Also consider pinning hot prefixes.
[08:30] Alex: for quantization, any guidance if we see padding blow-ups?
[08:34] Diego: use our pack-aware allocator and enable kernel-level packing option in runtime v4.2+. Also prefer 8-bit where memory allows; 4-bit is great for compute but increases fragmentation risk due to packing inefficiencies.
[08:47] Samira: driver versions? we run mixed GPU types.
[08:50] Diego: unify drivers is best, but runtime tolerates mixed GPUs. ensure latest CUDA and our compiled kernels targeted to lowest common compute capability. mismatched drivers can cause transient allocator regressions.
[09:05] Maria: Diego, let's open one of the customer's traces. Jordan, you uploaded the trace named aegis_kv_trace_20270812.json?
[09:12] Jordan: yes link in the S3 bucket under aegis/kv_traces.
[09:18] Diego: scanning... I see repeated pattern: page_fault_count spikes at 00:42 into session and eviction_count jumps. the interesting bit is many small allocations around similar offsets. that suggests the batcher is grouping requests with slightly different shifted contexts.
[09:36] Alex: there's also a spike in gpu_temp but not sustained.
[09:40] Diego: transient temp is normal under recompute. recompute plus page-in will increase SLO.
[09:45] Samira: what about re-compute costing us tokens? are we billed multiple times?
[09:50] Maria: if you run on Redwood Hosted you pay for compute per request as normal; re-compute increases token-level cost indirectly via GPU time. For Dedicated you factor it into throughput. we'll share cost-model examples.
[10:05] Jordan: we want a reproducible minimal test. what inputs should we vary?
[10:10] Diego: vary: 1) prefix share ratio (how many sessions share the same first N tokens), 2) divergence token position, 3) batcher settings (batch_time_ms, batch_max_tokens), 4) quantization (4-bit vs 8-bit), and 5) pinned prefixes on vs off. Run a sweep and capture kv_ metrics and page_fault_count.
[10:31] Alex: we can run that in our staging cluster. is the profiler intrusive?
[10:35] Diego: low overhead; it hooks into runtime metrics and captures traces for a few minutes at 1–2% perf hit. Dockerized script will be provided.
[10:44] Samira: about paging to NVMe — any recommendations on disk throughput?
[10:49] Diego: use NVMe with >2GB/s sustained for best page-in, but prefer host memory or NVLink where possible. If you must use NVMe, ensure queue depth tuning and async prefetching.
[11:01] Jordan: one more: we saw an odd case where cache entries were kept but attention outputs were wrong until restart. could that be stale kv bug?
[11:09] Diego: possible; we saw a bug in runtime v3.8 where under rare race conditions a freed kv pointer still referenced by a request could serve stale data. that was patched in v4.0. check your runtime version.
[11:22] Alex: we're on 3.7.2 — that might explain a few anomalies.
[11:26] Maria: upgrade path: we can assist with minimal-downtime upgrade playbook.
[11:32] Samira: ok great.
[11:36] Diego: final quick checklist: gather profiler traces, confirm runtime version, run the sweep with pinned vs unpinned prefixes, and capture batcher logs. we'll analyze and propose tuned config.
[11:49] Maria: recap — Maria to share docs and config, Diego to share scripts, Jordan to run traces, Samira to coordinate internal stake holders.
[11:59] Alex: thanks everyone.
[12:02] Maria: we'll follow up with calendar invite for the bench next week.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcript contains natural transcription noise (typos and speaker attribution may be slightly off). References: S3 link aegis/kv_traces, internal runtime versions v3.7.2 -> recommended v4.2+, perf script: /redwood/tools/kv_profiler (to be shared).
